problem: The claim that modular arithmetic "lets a computer handle 2048-bit numbers while storing only 2048 bits per value" is vacuous: any arithmetic stores 2048 bits for a 2048-bit value. The real point (intermediate products would grow to 4096 bits, reduction brings them back) is lost, so a student gets no idea why reduction matters.
fix: Say it plainly: a product of two 2048-bit numbers needs about 4096 bits, but reducing modulo n after each step keeps every stored value below n, that is, back to 2048 bits, so RSA stays cheap in memory.

problem: The ring of residues is written Zn in Section 1 and Z_n in the Section 2 heading, Q2 and Section 4. Two spellings for one object.
fix: Pick one form, for example Zn everywhere (or Z_n everywhere), and use it in headings, text and quiz answers.

problem: "Real cryptographic libraries never use the schoolbook method above" is misleading. Libraries do use square-and-multiply; what they replace is the modular multiplication/reduction inside it (Montgomery, Barrett). A student may conclude square-and-multiply is not used in practice.
fix: Write: libraries still use square-and-multiply, but replace the step "reduce modulo n by division" with Montgomery multiplication (multiplications and shifts) or Barrett reduction (precomputed reciprocal for a fixed modulus).

problem: "Barrett reduction for large batches" is vague and not the standard description.
fix: Say Barrett reduction is used when the same modulus is reused many times, because it precomputes a reciprocal and avoids a division per reduction.
